code.title: Thread-safe counter with a private lock

followUps: Thread-safe means every operation stays correct even when many threads run it at once, while immutable means the object can never change after it is built. Immutable objects are always thread-safe, but a thread-safe class can still be mutable. A ConcurrentHashMap changes all the time yet is safe because it guards its changes. Immutable is the easiest route: a String or a record with final fields needs no lock at all, since nobody can write to it.

A private lock object is better because outsiders cannot touch it, so only your class decides who waits. If you write synchronized(this), any caller can also do synchronized(yourObject) and hold your lock forever, or mix it into their own lock ordering and cause a deadlock. With private final Object lock = new Object() the locking rule becomes an internal detail you can change later. Cost: one extra small object per instance.

code.title: Opposite-direction transfers without deadlock (lock ordering)
code.python:
import threading

class Account:
    def __init__(self, id, balance):
        self.id = id
        self.balance = balance
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

def transfer(src, dst, amt):
    # Deadlock avoided: always lock the account with the smaller id first
    first, second = (src, dst) if src.id < dst.id else (dst, src)
    with first.lock:
        with second.lock:
            src.balance -= amt
            dst.balance += amt

a, b = Account(1, 1000), Account(2, 1000)
t1 = threading.Thread(target=lambda: [transfer(a, b, 10) for _ in range(100)])
t2 = threading.Thread(target=lambda: [transfer(b, a, 5) for _ in range(100)])
print("start A=1000 B=1000")
t1.start(); t2.start()
t1.join(); t2.join()  # opposite directions, no deadlock
print("end A=%d B=%d total=%d" % (a.balance, b.balance, a.balance + b.balance))

followUps: Run jstack <pid> (or jcmd <pid> Thread.print) and look for the line Found one Java-level deadlock; it lists each thread, the lock it holds and the lock it waits for. In code, call ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads(): it returns the ids of threads stuck in a cycle, or null if there is none. A watchdog can poll it every few seconds and log the stack traces, as the sample program does.

A livelock is when threads are not blocked but keep reacting to each other and make no progress. Picture two people in a corridor who both step aside the same way, again and again. In code, two threads that each release their lock on tryLock failure and retry at the same instant can repeat forever. The usual fix is a random back-off delay (jitter), or a fixed priority so one side always wins. Unlike a deadlock, the CPU stays busy.

code.title: synchronized vs ReentrantLock vs atomic, plus tryLock
code.python:
import threading

lock = threading.Lock()
lock_count = 0

class AtomicInt:
    """Python has no lock-free atomics; this wraps one tiny lock to show the API shape."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.v, self.m = 0, threading.Lock()
    def increment(self):
        with self.m:
            self.v += 1

atomic = AtomicInt()

def work():
    global lock_count
    for _ in range(1000):
        with lock:          # released automatically, even on exceptions
            lock_count += 1
        atomic.increment()

ts = [threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(4)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print("lock-guarded=%d atomic=%d" % (lock_count, atomic.v))

lock.acquire()  # hold the lock, then let another thread try with a timeout
def other():
    got = lock.acquire(timeout=0.05)  # tryLock with timeout: give up instead of waiting forever
    print("other thread tryLock while held: %s" % str(got).lower())
t = threading.Thread(target=other)
t.start(); t.join()
lock.release()

followUps: LongAdder is better when many threads update the same counter often and you only read the total now and then. AtomicLong keeps one value, so all threads fight over one memory cell with CAS retries. LongAdder spreads updates across several cells and adds them up on sum(). Example: 16 threads counting hits, 1 million increments each, runs several times faster. Downsides: sum() is not an exact snapshot while writers run, and it cannot do compareAndSet or return the new value.

ABA is when a CAS succeeds even though the value changed and changed back, so the check "still A" is true but the state is not the same. Example: a lock-free stack has top = A; thread 1 reads A and pauses; thread 2 pops A, pops B, pushes A back (now A points to something else); thread 1 CASes top from A to B and corrupts the stack. Fixes: AtomicStampedReference (value plus version number), or immutable nodes that are never reused. Garbage-collected Java makes it rare, but not impossible.

code.title: Compound map update: get-then-put vs merge

followUps: Because a null result from get would be ambiguous: it could mean the key is missing or the value is null, and in a concurrent map you cannot check containsKey afterwards, since another thread may have changed the map in between. Forbidding null removes the doubt: null always means absent. A normal HashMap has no such problem because a single thread can safely call containsKey next. Use Optional or a sentinel object if you need to store "no value".

The lambda runs while the map holds a lock on that bin, so slow or risky code there blocks every other thread that hashes to the same bin. Do not do I/O or call remote services in it. Do not touch the same map from inside it: computeIfAbsent that modifies the map can throw IllegalStateException or loop forever. Do not take other locks, which can cause a deadlock. Keep it short, pure and quick, and for slow loading store a CompletableFuture as the value instead.

code.title: Token bucket with injected clock and Retry-After
code.python:
import threading

class Bucket:
    """Token bucket in milli-tokens: 1 request costs 1000, refill 1 milli-token per ms."""
    def __init__(self, cap_tokens, now):
        self.capacity = cap_tokens * 1000
        self.cost = 1000
        self.tokens = self.capacity
        self.last = now
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def try_acquire(self, now):
        with self.lock:  # refill + check + take in one critical section
            self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (now - self.last))  # lazy refill
            self.last = now
            if self.tokens >= self.cost:
                self.tokens -= self.cost
                return 0
            return self.cost - self.tokens  # ms until next token = Retry-After

b = Bucket(3, 0)  # burst 3, 1 token per second
for t in [0, 0, 0, 0, 500, 1000, 1500, 2500, 3000]:  # injected fake clock (ms)
    wait = b.try_acquire(t)
    print("t=%dms %s" % (t, "allow" if wait == 0 else "deny retryAfter=%dms" % wait))

followUps: When a request is denied, compute how long until one token is available and send that as the Retry-After header (in seconds, rounded up), together with HTTP 429. In the sample, with 0 tokens left and a refill rate of 1 token per second, the wait is 1000 ms, and with 500 milli-tokens left it is 500 ms. Formula: (cost - tokens) / ratePerMs. Compute it inside the same critical section as the check, so the number matches the state that caused the denial.

currentTimeMillis follows the wall clock, which can jump forward or backward when NTP or an admin adjusts it. A jump back gives negative elapsed time and a stuck bucket; a jump forward refills it with a flood of free tokens. Use a monotonic clock (System.nanoTime, time.monotonic, steady_clock), which only moves forward, and hide it behind an injectable Clock so tests can use a fake one. The monotonic value is only good for measuring differences, not for printing dates.

Use two buckets per key: one counts requests per minute, one counts tokens per minute. Before a call you only know an estimate (prompt length plus the max output tokens you asked for), so reserve that many tokens with tryAcquire(estimate). After the response, read the real usage and refund the difference (or charge the extra). Example: limit 90,000 tokens/min; a call reserves 4,000, uses 1,500, so 2,500 goes back. Cost per call is O(1) with one lock per key.

code.title: Fixed window vs sliding log vs sliding counter at a boundary burst
code.python:
from collections import deque

W, N = 1000, 5
times = [900] * 5 + [1100] * 5
fixed, log, ctr = [0, 0], [0, 0], [0, 0]
counts = {}          # fixed window: one counter per window
stamps = deque()     # sliding log: accepted timestamps
prev = cur = cur_win = 0  # sliding counter: two numbers
for i, t in enumerate(times):
    burst, win = (0 if i < 5 else 1), t // W
    c = counts.get(win, 0)
    if c < N:
        counts[win] = c + 1
        fixed[burst] += 1
    while stamps and stamps[0] <= t - W:   # evict old
        stamps.popleft()
    if len(stamps) < N:                    # only accepted requests are stored
        stamps.append(t)
        log[burst] += 1
    if win != cur_win:
        prev = cur if win == cur_win + 1 else 0
        cur, cur_win = 0, win
    est = prev * (W - t % W) // W + cur    # weighted estimate
    if est < N:
        cur += 1
        ctr[burst] += 1
print("burst of 5 at t=900, burst of 5 at t=1100 (limit 5 per 1000ms)")
print("fixed window   allowed: %d then %d" % tuple(fixed))
print("sliding log    allowed: %d then %d" % tuple(log))
print("sliding counter allowed: %d then %d" % tuple(ctr))

followUps: For OTP sends pick the sliding window log: the limit is tiny (say 3 per 10 minutes), so storing 3 timestamps per phone number costs almost nothing, and exactness matters because each SMS costs money and abuse is the risk. For a public API at internet scale pick the sliding window counter (or a token bucket): it needs only two numbers per key, so millions of keys fit in memory, and a small error at the window edge is acceptable. Fixed window is fine only for rough protection.

It behaves correctly: the estimate drops to the current window's count. If the previous window is two or more windows old, the weighted previous count must be treated as 0, because that data is stale. In the sample code, prev = (win == curWin + 1) ? cur : 0 does exactly that. Without this reset, the counter would still weigh old traffic into the estimate and wrongly deny a client that was quiet for a long time. Both counters are then O(1) to update.

code.title: Bounded producer-consumer with a poison pill
code.python:
import queue
import threading

q = queue.Queue(maxsize=2)  # bounded: put() blocks when full
POISON = -1                  # tells the consumer to stop
seen = []

def consumer():
    while True:
        v = q.get()          # blocks when empty
        if v == POISON:
            break
        seen.append(v)

def producer():
    for i in range(1, 6):
        q.put(i)             # backpressure when consumer is slow
    q.put(POISON)            # one pill per consumer

c = threading.Thread(target=consumer)
p = threading.Thread(target=producer)
c.start(); p.start()
p.join(); c.join()
print("produced 1..5, capacity 2")
print("consumed in order [%s] sum=%d" % (", ".join(map(str, seen)), sum(seen)))

followUps: Because a queue has two ends that mostly touch different nodes: producers append at the tail and consumers remove from the head. With a separate putLock and takeLock, a producer and a consumer can work at the same time instead of waiting for each other, which roughly doubles throughput under load. An atomic count keeps the two sides in sync, and a signal crosses over when the queue turns empty or non-empty. ArrayBlockingQueue uses one lock because its array is shared.

Start from the rule: a bounded queue exists to limit memory and to push back on fast producers. A small capacity (10 to 100) keeps latency low and shows slow consumers quickly; a bigger one absorbs bursts. Estimate: if bursts are 500 items and consumers drain 100 per second, capacity near 500 avoids blocking producers. Never use unbounded queues for work that can pile up, since a slow consumer then ends in OutOfMemoryError. Measure queue depth and tune with real traffic.

code.title: LRU cache where get also takes the lock
code.python:
import threading
from collections import OrderedDict

class LruCache:
    def __init__(self, cap):
        self.cap = cap
        self.map = OrderedDict()      # order = oldest first, newest last
        self.lock = threading.Lock()  # get() relinks, so get needs the lock too

    def get(self, k):
        with self.lock:
            if k not in self.map:
                return "null"
            self.map.move_to_end(k)   # mark as most recently used
            return self.map[k]

    def put(self, k, v):
        with self.lock:
            self.map[k] = v
            self.map.move_to_end(k)
            if len(self.map) > self.cap:
                self.map.popitem(last=False)  # evict the least recently used

    def keys(self):
        with self.lock:
            return "[" + ", ".join(self.map) + "]"

c = LruCache(2)
c.put("a", 1); c.put("b", 2)
print("get a -> %s" % c.get("a"))   # a becomes most recent
c.put("c", 3)                        # evicts b
print("get b -> %s" % c.get("b"))
c.put("d", 4)                        # evicts a
print("get a -> %s" % c.get("a"))
print("get c -> %s" % c.get("c"))
print("keys oldest to newest: %s" % c.keys())

followUps: Store an expiry time in each entry (for example expiresAt = now + ttl). On get, if now >= expiresAt treat it as a miss and remove it (lazy expiry). Add a periodic sweep, or Caffeine's expireAfterWrite, so entries nobody reads do not sit in memory. Use an injected clock so tests can check it. Example: ttl 60 s, entry stored at t=0, read at t=61 gives a miss and a reload. Cost: one long per entry, still O(1) per operation.

A stampede happens when a popular key expires and hundreds of threads all miss at once, and all hit the database to reload the same value. Prevent it with single-flight: keep a map of key to an in-flight CompletableFuture; the first thread starts the load, the others wait for that same future. Other tools are a short random jitter on TTLs so keys do not expire together, and serving the stale value while one thread refreshes it. Result: 1 database call instead of 500.

code.title: O(1) LFU with frequency buckets and minFreq
code.python:
import threading
from collections import OrderedDict

class Lfu:
    """O(1) LFU: key->value, key->freq, freq->keys in insertion order, plus min_freq."""
    def __init__(self, cap):
        self.cap, self.min_freq = cap, 0
        self.val, self.freq, self.buckets = {}, {}, {}
        self.lock = threading.Lock()  # several structures change together, so one lock

    def _touch(self, k):
        f = self.freq[k]
        del self.buckets[f][k]
        if not self.buckets[f] and f == self.min_freq:
            self.min_freq += 1        # old minimum bucket emptied
        self.freq[k] = f + 1
        self.buckets.setdefault(f + 1, OrderedDict())[k] = True

    def get(self, k):
        with self.lock:
            if k not in self.val:
                return -1
            self._touch(k)
            return self.val[k]

    def put(self, k, v):
        with self.lock:
            if self.cap == 0:
                return
            if k in self.val:
                self.val[k] = v
                self._touch(k)
                return
            if len(self.val) == self.cap:  # evict oldest key in the lowest-frequency bucket
                victim = next(iter(self.buckets[self.min_freq]))
                del self.buckets[self.min_freq][victim]
                del self.val[victim]
                del self.freq[victim]
            self.val[k], self.freq[k] = v, 1
            self.buckets.setdefault(1, OrderedDict())[k] = True
            self.min_freq = 1

c = Lfu(2)
c.put(1, 1); c.put(2, 2)
out = [c.get(1)]      # freq of 1 is now 2
c.put(3, 3)           # evicts 2 (lowest freq)
out += [c.get(2), c.get(3)]
c.put(4, 4)           # 1 and 3 tie at freq 2, evicts older (1)
out += [c.get(1), c.get(3), c.get(4)]
print("capacity 2 results: [" + ", ".join(map(str, out)) + "]")

followUps: Because frequency counts only grow, an item that was hot last month keeps a high count forever and blocks new items from staying. Example: an old key with 10,000 hits sits in the cache while a new popular key with 50 hits is always the one evicted. Aging fixes this by halving all counts every so often, or after N accesses, which is what TinyLFU does with a small counter sketch. Then old popularity fades and the cache adapts to what is hot now.

Run many threads doing random put and get, then check the invariants that should always hold: size never above capacity, every key in the value map is in exactly one frequency bucket, the frequency map and the buckets agree, and minFreq points at a non-empty bucket. Add a debug method checkInvariants() and call it at the end (and sometimes during the run under the same lock). Also compare against a simple single-threaded model run on the same operation log when order is controlled.

code.title: All-or-nothing seat booking with ordered per-seat locks

followUps: Treat the late callback as a payment that has no seat. First check the hold atomically: if the seat is still free or still held by that user, extend and confirm it; if someone else booked it, you cannot give it back, so refund automatically and tell the user. Make the callback idempotent by keying it on a payment id, since gateways retry. Example: hold expires at 10:05, the callback comes at 10:06, seat now belongs to user B, so the payment is refunded in full. Keep the hold a little longer than the payment timeout to make this rare.

ABA is when a CAS sees the expected value but the seat went AVAILABLE, then HELD, then AVAILABLE again, so the check passes though history changed. For seats it is mostly harmless, because a CAS from AVAILABLE to HELD only cares that the seat is free right now. It becomes a risk if you reuse the same state object, so each hold should be a fresh immutable object with its own user and expiry time, or carry a version number. Then a stale reference never matches by accident.

Put users in a queue before the booking service. Give each person a ticket number on arrival, let a fixed number in (for example 500 per minute) by moving them to a short-lived admitted token, and show everyone else their position. The booking service accepts only admitted tokens, so its load stays flat no matter how many people arrive. Store the queue in Redis (a sorted set by arrival time). Admitted tokens expire after a few minutes so idle users free their place, and the seat locks still protect correctness.

code.title: Detecting a deadlock with ThreadMXBean
code.python:
import threading

# Python has no built-in deadlock detector, so a watchdog uses lock timeouts:
# a thread that cannot get its second lock in time reports itself as stuck.
a, b = threading.Lock(), threading.Lock()
barrier = threading.Barrier(2)  # make the bad interleaving certain
stuck = []

def worker(name, first, second):
    with first:
        barrier.wait()                               # both threads now hold their first lock
        if second.acquire(timeout=0.3):              # tryLock with timeout
            second.release()
        else:
            stuck.append(name)                       # circular wait: report instead of hanging

ts = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=("worker-1", a, b)),   # A then B
      threading.Thread(target=worker, args=("worker-2", b, a))]   # B then A
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print("deadlock detected: %s" % str(len(stuck) > 0).lower())
print("threads in the cycle: %d" % len(stuck))
print("fix: acquire locks in one global order (e.g. by id)")

followUps: Yes, but in a different form. A CAS loop cannot be deadlocked since nobody waits holding a lock, but it can livelock or starve: if threads keep changing the value so that another thread's CAS always fails, that thread retries forever. Lock-free means some thread always makes progress, not every thread. Fix with back-off, a bounded retry count with fallback to a lock, or a wait-free design. Example: with 2 threads one wins each round, so the system advances though one may lose many times.

Because you do not control what the listener does. It may be slow, throw, or take its own locks, and if that lock is held by a thread waiting for yours you get a deadlock. It can also call back into your object (re-entrancy) and see half-updated state. The safe pattern: under the lock, change state and copy the list of listeners and the event data; release the lock; then call the listeners. The cost is a small copy, and events may arrive slightly after the state change.

code.title: Capping concurrency with a Semaphore on virtual threads
code.python:
import threading
import time

limit = threading.BoundedSemaphore(3)  # cap concurrent calls to a downstream service
lock = threading.Lock()
running = max_seen = done = 0

def task():
    global running, max_seen, done
    with limit:                         # waits here when 3 calls are already running
        with lock:
            running += 1
            max_seen = max(max_seen, running)
        time.sleep(0.02)                # pretend remote call
        with lock:
            running -= 1
    with lock:
        done += 1

ts = [threading.Thread(target=task) for _ in range(20)]  # Java 21 would use cheap virtual threads here
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join()
print("tasks completed: %d" % done)
print("max concurrent calls <= 3: %s" % str(max_seen <= 3).lower())

followUps: Use a Semaphore with N permits and wrap each call in acquire() and release() in a finally. With virtual threads you can start thousands of tasks, but only N reach the provider at once; the others wait cheaply. Example: provider allows 8 concurrent requests, so new Semaphore(8). For a limit on tokens per minute, combine it with a token bucket. Do not shrink an executor pool for this, because pooling virtual threads defeats their purpose.

Not slower in itself, but on Java 21 it can hurt scaling: if a virtual thread blocks inside a synchronized block (for example on I/O or take()), it pins its carrier thread, so that OS thread cannot run other virtual threads. With few carriers (default = CPU cores) many pinned tasks stall the program. Fix: use ReentrantLock around blocking code, or run on JDK 24 or later, where monitors no longer pin in most cases. Short synchronized sections with no blocking are fine.

code.title: Stress test with a start latch and bounded waits
code.python:
import threading

class Bank:
    """Class under test: total money must never change."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.bal = [500, 500]
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
    def move(self, src, dst, amt):
        with self.lock:
            self.bal[src] -= amt
            self.bal[dst] += amt
    def total(self):
        with self.lock:
            return self.bal[0] + self.bal[1]

bank = Bank()
threads, iters = 8, 5000
go = threading.Barrier(threads)  # all threads start together so they collide

def worker(direction):
    go.wait()
    for _ in range(iters):
        bank.move(direction, 1 - direction, 1)

ts = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(t % 2,)) for t in range(threads)]
for t in ts: t.start()
for t in ts: t.join(10)          # bounded wait: a hang becomes a failure, not a stuck build
print("invariant total == 1000: %s" % str(bank.total() == 1000 and not any(t.is_alive() for t in ts)).lower())
print("4 threads each way, net change per side = 0: %s" % str(bank.bal == [500, 500]).lower())

followUps: Linearizability means every operation seems to take effect at one instant between its start and its end, and the order of those instants matches a valid single-threaded history. If thread A finishes put(x,1) before thread B starts get(x), B must see 1 (or something newer). It is the strongest common correctness rule for concurrent objects. Tools such as Lincheck record the real call history and search for such an order; if none exists, the object has a bug.

Because races depend on the exact timing of threads, and a test may run through only a tiny part of all possible interleavings. A bug that needs a thread to pause for 50 nanoseconds in a precise spot might happen once in a million runs, or only on a machine with more cores, or with a different JIT state. Passing shows you did not hit the bug, not that it is absent. Run on several machines with many iterations, vary thread counts, add random yields, and use tools like jcstress that cover interleavings on purpose.
